newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Socialists to try to hang on to power.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Socialists to try to hang on to power.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists, spurning 27 days of opposition street demonstrations to demand elections, said they would go ahead with plans to form a new government.

Students and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) vowed to intensify their protests, and disrupt road and rail links further, if the formerly communist Socialists did hold onto power instead of opting for immediate elections.

Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov said in a television interview on Saturday: "I'm sure next week Bulgaria will have a new government but it is hard to predict what the future of this government will be."
He said Nikolai Dobrev, who has a mandate to form the next government, would become prime minister the 240-seat parliament approved his cabinet.
Bulgaria has had a caretaker government, unable to take action in the face of a deep economic crisis, since December when prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned.
Parvanov said the Socialists could count on 122 votes in parliament, an absolute majority which meant that they could win the required confidence vote.

"I think that the anti-crisis programme which is proposed by Nikolai Dobrev is quite constructive but will still need about 30 to 40 days to implement and to regain the confidence of the people," he said.

He said Bulgaria must have a government immediately to pass legislation to halt a collapse in the value of the lev, the national currency, and cope with an inflation rate which has hit 50 percent a month and is still rising.
The Socialists say they will hold general elections, not due until December 1998, later this year but their offer has failed to satisfy the opposition, which wants the vote held now.
The Socialist party's supreme council will hold special talks with its parliamentary deputies and coalition partners on Sunday at a meeting which is expected to choose ministers for a new cabinet.
But there have been signs of party splits and a reluctunce by some party members to join a new government in view of the mass opposition street demonstrations.
Thousands of opposition supporters, workers and students, blaming the Socialists for the economic collapse, have staged daily anti-government rallies to demand elections now.
Festive protesters, including entire families, pensioners and students, streamed through Sofia on Saturday, blowing horns, banging drums and carrying banners proclaiming: "I am not a slave."

"We think that victory is very close," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told the cheering throng in the square outside Alexander Nevski Orthodox cathedral, hours before Parvanov expressed his determination to have a new Socialist government.

Several thousand UDF supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fourth day. Protesters burned tyres in the highway at Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, as about 100 riot police stood nearby.
Kostov warned the Socialists that similar disruptions would sweep the country if they voted in a new cabinet instead of calling elections.
"The Socialists should consider this an example of what will happen if they pass a government through parliament," he said. "The Doupnitsa road and rail blockades will become nationwide actions."
